title: The system: a hotel booking platform on one PostgreSQL primary
caption: Every booking commits on one primary and reaches a standby before it is confirmed; replicas, the WAL archive and CDC all feed from the same write-ahead log.

steps.text: A guest books two nights. The API servers are stateless and scale out; each one talks SQL to the pooler, which multiplexes thousands of client connections onto ~150 server connections.
The pooler sends the write transaction to the primary: lock the room-night rows, insert the booking, decrement availability, COMMIT. All of it happens, or none of it.
The commit is acknowledged only after the sync standby has flushed its WAL record (~1 ms in the same region), so a confirmed booking survives losing the primary's disk.
Read replicas replay the same WAL a few ms behind. Browsing hotels and past trips go there; the booking page itself reads from the primary.
Every WAL segment is shipped to object storage next to a nightly base backup: any second of the last 14 days can be restored (point-in-time recovery).
Logical decoding turns committed changes into an ordered stream; CDC updates the search index and the warehouse, so the API never writes to three systems at once.

scenarios.name: Holiday sale
scenarios.summary: Traffic jumps 20× for an hour: the pooler protects the primary from connection storms and replicas absorb the browsing.

steps.text: The API autoscales from 20 to 400 pods; each wants 10 connections, 4 000 in total.
The pooler still opens only ~150 server connections and queues the rest for a few ms. Without it, 4 000 backend processes would eat the primary's memory.
90% of the extra load is searching and browsing: it lands on replicas (add one more in minutes).
Writes grow only 3×, well within one primary. Search catches up through CDC with a second of lag.

scenarios.name: Replica falls behind
scenarios.summary: A long report on the replica and a write burst push lag to 40 s: route reads away from it instead of serving stale availability.

steps.text: An analyst's 10-minute report runs on the replica while a bulk price update hits the primary.
Replay pauses behind the report's snapshot; lag reaches 40 s. Guests would see rooms that are already gone.
The pooler's health check reads replay lag and stops sending reads to that replica above 5 s.
Fix the cause: reports move to the warehouse (fed by CDC), and the replica catches up.

scenarios.name: Schema migration
scenarios.summary: Adding an index to a 2 TB bookings table can block every write; online variants and lock timeouts keep the site up.

steps.text: A deploy runs a plain CREATE INDEX on bookings. It holds a lock that blocks inserts for the whole build.
Booking requests pile up in the pooler, and then in the API, until they time out.
Safe version: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, SET lock_timeout = '2s', add columns as nullable and backfill in small batches.
The change replays on standby and replicas; CDC consumers must accept the new column before it is written.
